lead: Pneumatic power is compressed air or gas used to do work. On most aircraft it is bleed air, taken from an engine compressor and regulated, so the aircraft does not need a separate compressor for every job: that air drives cabin cooling and pressurisation, clears ice from the wing and intake, and spins the engine during start. A few aircraft also carry a high-pressure pneumatic power system of stored compressed air or nitrogen for gear, brakes and emergencies.
prereq: You need: hydraulic systems for how valves and actuators are driven, and cabin pressurisation and air cycle cooling for what happens to the air after it leaves the manifold.

blocks.text: An engine compressor raises the pressure and temperature of air before combustion. A small fraction of that air is taken out through a bleed port and sent to the aircraft. Pressure at the port depends on which compressor stage is tapped and on engine power. A low-pressure (LP) port gives cooler air at moderate pressure. A high-pressure (HP) port gives higher pressure but hotter air.

At low engine power the LP stage cannot supply enough pressure. The HP valve opens and HP air feeds the system. As power rises, LP pressure becomes enough; the HP valve closes and a check valve stops HP air from flowing backwards into the LP duct. So the source switches with power, and bleed is not always available from the HP stage.

Three sources feed the manifold: engine bleed (HP or LP), the auxiliary power unit (APU) on the ground and during engine start, and a ground cart connected at a ground service port. Before cooling, bleed air may sit at a few hundred kPa and a few hundred degrees Celsius.

The first heat exchanger is the precooler. Fan air passes on one side and hot bleed on the other. The precooler lowers the bleed temperature, but the air leaving it is still hot enough to need heat protection on ducts. A fan-air valve controls the cooling flow.

Next is the pressure regulating and shut-off valve (PRV). The PRV regulates the downstream pressure to a design value, usually a few hundred kPa, and can close fully to shut off the bleed. It is controlled by a bleed monitoring computer that reads pressure and temperature sensors in the duct.

The regulated air enters a manifold: a network of ducts that runs along the fuselage. Check valves allow flow from a source into the manifold but block reverse flow, so a failed engine bleed cannot pressurise another engine's ducts. Isolation valves split the manifold into sections. If one section leaks, the crew can close an isolation valve and keep the other engine supplying the remaining users.

Protection is layered. For overpressure, the PRV closes and a relief valve opens if the PRV fails. For overheat, duct sensors trip a warning and close the affected valve. The crew sees the fault on the bleed panel or the electronic centralised aircraft monitor (ECAM), depending on the aircraft.
The manifold feeds several users, each through its own valve:

items: Air conditioning packs take bleed air and cool it; see air cycle cooling.
Wing and engine anti-ice use hot bleed air to keep surfaces above freezing; see ice and rain protection.
Engine starting uses bleed air to turn the air turbine starter; see engine starting.
Hydraulic reservoirs and potable water tanks are pressurised with bleed air, to stop pump cavitation and to deliver water.
On some types door seals are inflated with bleed air.

blocks.text: Cabin pressure is not a bleed user of its own: the packs feed the cabin and the outflow valve sets its pressure.

On a typical twin-engine aircraft, either engine can supply the whole manifold through the isolation valves. The APU supplies the manifold on the ground when engines are off; its air joins downstream of the precooler and the PRV, so no engine fan air is needed to cool it. This shared manifold is why a single bleed leak can affect several systems, and why isolation valves matter.

blocks.text: Some turboprops and older transports use a separate pneumatic power system at about 1000 to 3300 psi for landing gear, wheel brakes, nose-wheel steering and propeller braking. Many more aircraft carry only an emergency nitrogen or air bottle that can blow the gear down or apply the brakes once when the hydraulics have failed. A stored gas is light, does not catch fire and needs no return line, but it is compressible, so it suits on-off jobs rather than fine position control.

items: An engine-driven multi-stage piston compressor raises the air pressure; a relief valve protects each stage.
A moisture separator and a chemical dryer remove water, which would freeze in valves at altitude; a filter removes dirt.
Storage bottles hold the charge; a back-pressure valve keeps the compressor loaded until the bottles are charged.
A pressure-reducing valve gives each user the lower pressure it needs, and a shuttle valve switches a user, such as a brake, from its normal supply to the emergency bottle.

blocks.where: p is absolute pressure and V is gas volume; a bottle that discharges into empty actuators shares its gas over the larger volume, so its pressure falls in proportion.

examples.question: A bleed duct carries 0.30 kg/s of air at 250 kPa and 200 °C. The duct area is 0.010 m². Take R = 287 J/(kg·K). Find the air density and the mean velocity.
steps: Convert temperature to kelvin: T = 200 + 273 = 473 K.
Convert pressure to pascal: p = 250 kPa = 250 000 Pa.
Apply the ideal-gas relation: ρ = p/(R × T) = 250 000/(287 × 473).
Use mass flow: ṁ = ρ × A × v, so v = ṁ/(ρ × A).
examples.answer: The density is 1.84 kg/m³ and the mean velocity is 16.29 m/s.
examples.check:
p = 250000.0
T = 473.0
R = 287.0
mdot = 0.30
A = 0.010
rho = p/(R*T)
v = mdot/(rho*A)
print(round(rho, 2))
print(round(v, 2))

examples.question: An emergency gear-extension bottle holds 2.5 L of nitrogen at 200 bar and 15 °C. When it is fired, the gas fills the bottle plus the lines and actuators, which add 9.5 L. Each actuator needs at least 30 bar to push its leg into the downlock. Take R = 296.8 J/(kg·K) for nitrogen and the temperature as constant. Find the final pressure, say whether it is enough, and find the mass of gas in the bottle.
steps: Total volume after discharge: V₂ = 2.5 + 9.5 = 12.0 L.
Boyle’s law: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = 200 × 2.5 ÷ 12.0 = 41.7 bar.
Compare: 41.7 bar is above the 30 bar the actuators need, a margin of 11.7 bar, so the bottle can extend the gear once.
examples.answer: The gas settles at 41.7 bar, enough for one extension with 11.7 bar to spare; the bottle holds 0.585 kg of nitrogen.

traps: Do not write that bleed air normally comes from the HP stage. The HP port feeds the system only at low engine power; at cruise and climb power the LP port is enough and the HP valve stays closed.
Using gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure in ρ = p/(RT). The formula needs absolute pressure in Pa and absolute temperature in K.
Thinking the isolation valve is a check valve. A check valve is one-way and automatic; an isolation valve is opened or closed by command to split the manifold.
A duct overheat or leak closes the bleed and isolation valves for that section, not the pack valve alone; the pack valve only stops flow into one pack.
Use absolute pressure in p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ and in ρ = p/(RT); with gauge values the answer is wrong, most of all at low pressure.

quiz.q: Name the two engine compressor bleed sources.
quiz.a: The low-pressure (LP) stage and the high-pressure (HP) stage.

quiz.q: Why is a precooler fitted before the manifold?
quiz.a: It uses fan air to reduce the bleed temperature so ducts and valves are not overheated; the air is still hot after it.

quiz.q: A duct carries 0.24 kg/s of air of density 1.80 kg/m³ through an area of 0.008 m². Find the mean velocity.
Why does the HP bleed valve close at high engine power?
quiz.a: At high power the LP stage pressure is already enough. Keeping the HP valve closed avoids taking hotter, higher-energy air than needed, which would cost fuel and overload the precooler; the check valve stops HP air flowing back into the LP duct whenever the HP valve is open.

quiz.q: What is the job of an isolation valve in the bleed manifold?
quiz.a: It splits the manifold into sections so a leak or failed source can be isolated while the other engine supplies the remaining users.

quiz.q: A duct overheat warning appears. What does the bleed system do, and why?
quiz.a: The duct sensor trips a warning and the affected bleed valve closes, stopping hot air from reaching the overheated section.

quiz.q: An emergency brake bottle of 1.0 L at 150 bar discharges into lines and brake pistons of 2.0 L. Find the final pressure at constant temperature.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Boeing 787 uses a bleedless architecture: electric compressors supply the cabin, and engine bleed is kept only for engine cowl anti-icing. Research continues toward more-electric aircraft, where hydraulic and pneumatic loads become electrical. Bleed duct leaks are found by loop sensors along the duct. Search terms: bleedless architecture, bleed monitoring computer, bleed leak detection, more-electric aircraft.
